clinicalPearls: Caused by reactivation of BK polyomavirus, a ubiquitous virus latent in the urinary tract epithelium that reactivates under the intense immunosuppression of kidney transplantation
It is a leading infectious cause of allograft dysfunction and loss, typically emerging within the first year after transplantation
Usually silent until an asymptomatic rise in serum creatinine appears; frank cystitis or ureteric stenosis is less common than in haemorrhagic cystitis after stem-cell transplant
Urine cytology may reveal decoy cells, tubular epithelial cells bearing enlarged nuclei with ground-glass viral inclusions that mimic malignant cells
Surveillance uses quantitative plasma BK virus DNA (viraemia), which correlates with nephropathy better than urinary viral load alone
Definitive diagnosis requires allograft biopsy showing viral cytopathic changes in tubular cells with confirmatory SV40 large T antigen immunostaining
The cornerstone of management is judicious reduction of immunosuppression to allow virus-specific cellular immunity to recover, balanced against the risk of rejection
reference.pathophysiology: BK polyomavirus infects most people in childhood and thereafter persists latently within the epithelium of the renal tubules and urinary tract. In the transplanted kidney, heavy pharmacological immunosuppression allows the virus to reactivate and replicate, first producing viruria, then viraemia, and finally invasive infection of tubular epithelial cells. Lytic viral replication causes cell injury and denudation of the tubular basement membrane, with an accompanying interstitial inflammatory infiltrate and progressive tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. The inflammatory response is difficult to distinguish histologically from acute rejection, and untreated infection leads to scarring and irreversible loss of graft function. Ureteric involvement can cause stenosis and obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructive uropathy or ureteric stenosis from other causes
Recurrent or de novo glomerular disease in the graft
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma BK virus DNA by PCR for screening and monitoring of viraemia
Urine BK virus DNA quantification and urine cytology for decoy cells
Renal allograft biopsy with SV40 large T antigen immunohistochemistry
Serial serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate
Assessment of net immunosuppression, including drug levels of calcineurin inhibitors and antiproliferative agents
Imaging of the urinary tract to exclude ureteric stenosis or obstruction
redFlags: Rising allograft creatinine with high-level BK viraemia
Biopsy features overlapping with acute rejection creating diagnostic and therapeutic conflict
Ureteric stenosis with obstructive graft dysfunction
Persistent high viral load despite reduction of immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on how early infection is detected and immunosuppression reduced; caught during viraemia the graft is often preserved, but established nephropathy with extensive fibrosis frequently progresses to allograft failure despite intervention.
pitfalls: Mistaking BK nephropathy for acute rejection and intensifying immunosuppression, which worsens viral replication
Relying on urinary viral load or decoy cells alone, which are sensitive but not specific for invasive nephropathy
Delaying protocol screening so that infection is only detected once irreversible scarring has occurred
Reducing immunosuppression too aggressively and precipitating rejection
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
